title: Transponders, ADS-B & Radar Services

required_knowledge_points.title: Radar Services — Primary vs. Secondary Radar and Flight Following
required_knowledge_points.why: The DPE asks: 'What is the difference between primary and secondary radar?' and 'What are the limitations of Flight Following?' Primary radar sees everything — it bounces radio waves off metal. Secondary radar requires a transponder — it asks the aircraft who it is. Flight Following is advisory, workload-permitting, and does NOT clear you into Class B.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: PRIMARY RADAR: operates on radio wave reflection — a high-energy pulse bounces off the aircraft's metallic skin ('skin paint') and returns to the receiver. Measures distance and azimuth. Requires NO equipment in the aircraft. Limitations: affected by weather clutter, ground clutter, and range limitations. SECONDARY RADAR (ATCRBS): sends an interrogation pulse; the aircraft's transponder actively replies with a discrete squawk code and altitude data. Vastly more reliable, greater range, eliminates clutter. Requires a cooperative transponder. ATC fuses both primary and secondary returns to build the composite traffic picture. VFR FLIGHT FOLLOWING: advisory service provided by ARTCC (Center) or TRACON on a workload-permitting basis. What you get: traffic advisories (12-o'clock format based on radar ground track, NOT magnetic heading), safety alerts, and a discrete squawk code. What you DON'T get: terrain clearance, weather avoidance, or guaranteed coverage. ATC can terminate at any time due to IFR workload. CLOCK POSITION TRAP: ATC issues traffic calls based on the aircraft's radar ground track. In a strong crosswind with a significant crab angle, traffic called at '12 o'clock' may appear out the SIDE window. CLASS B CLEARANCE: Flight Following does NOT equal Class B clearance. The pilot must hear the explicit phrase 'Cleared into the Class Bravo airspace' before penetrating the boundary. TRSA: Terminal Radar Service Area — voluntary radar environment around certain Class D airports. VFR participation is encouraged but legally optional.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Primary vs. Secondary Radar
| Feature | Primary Radar | Secondary Radar (ATCRBS) |
|---|---|---|
| **How it works** | Bounces radio waves off aircraft skin | Sends interrogation, aircraft transponder replies |
| **Aircraft equipment** | None required | Transponder required |
| **Data provided** | Distance + azimuth only | Squawk code + altitude + ID |
| **Weather/ground clutter** | ❌ Affected | ✅ Eliminated |
| **Range** | Limited | Much greater |

### VFR Flight Following
| You GET | You DON'T GET |
|---|---|
| Traffic advisories (clock position) | Terrain clearance |
| Safety alerts | Weather avoidance |
| Discrete squawk code | Guaranteed continuous coverage |
| — | Class B clearance |

### Clock Position Trap
- ATC traffic calls = based on **radar ground track**
- In crosswind (crab angle): traffic at '12 o'clock' may appear **out the side window**
- Always verify: scan WIDER than the reported clock position

> ⚠️ **Checkride Trap:** Flight Following ≠ Class B clearance. You need the **exact words** 'Cleared into the Class Bravo airspace.' Anything less is NOT a clearance.

required_knowledge_points.title: Transponder Modes and ADS-B — Mandates, Airspace, and the 10,000-Foot Rule
required_knowledge_points.why: The DPE asks: 'Where is ADS-B Out required?' and 'Explain the Mode C veil.' The airspace mandates are testable, precise, and have traps — especially the 2,500 ft AGL exclusion for the 10,000 ft MSL rule.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: TRANSPONDER MODES: Mode A = 4-digit squawk code for identification. Mode C = squawk code + pressure altitude from blind encoder (referenced to 29.92 inHg, ATC computer corrects to local altimeter). Mode S = Mode A/C + unique 24-bit ICAO address + selective interrogation. Forms backbone of TCAS. ADS-B OUT: 'Automatic' (no pilot input), 'Dependent' (relies on aircraft GPS), 'Surveillance' (replaces radar), 'Broadcast' (transmits continuously). Broadcasts GPS position, altitude, velocity, Flight ID every second. Two frequencies: 1090ES (Mode S transponder, required at/above FL180 and internationally) and 978 MHz UAT (below 18,000 ft MSL, US only). WHERE REQUIRED (91.215/91.225): Class A, B, and C airspace. Within the 30-NM Mode C veil surrounding primary Class B airports. Class E airspace at and above 10,000 ft MSL. THE 10,000 FT EXCLUSION: the requirement excludes airspace at and below 2,500 ft AGL. This means: if terrain is 9,000 ft MSL and the aircraft is at 11,000 ft MSL (2,000 ft AGL), NO transponder/ADS-B is required — despite being above 10,000 ft MSL. This accommodates mountainous operations. FLIGHT ID (HAYSLETT 2017): the ADS-B Flight ID must match the call sign filed on the flight plan. For GA = N-number. A call sign mismatch triggers a regulatory violation. EXEMPTIONS: gliders, balloons, and aircraft without engine-driven electrical systems are exempt from transponder/ADS-B requirements when outside actual Class B/C airspace (even within the Mode C veil).
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Transponder Modes
| Mode | What It Transmits |
|---|---|
| **Mode A** | 4-digit squawk code (identification only) |
| **Mode C** | Squawk code + pressure altitude (blind encoder, 29.92 ref) |
| **Mode S** | Mode A/C + unique ICAO address + selective interrogation |

### ADS-B Out
- **Broadcasts:** GPS position, altitude, velocity, Flight ID
- **Update rate:** Every 1 second
- **1090ES:** Required at/above FL180 and internationally
- **978 UAT:** US only, below 18,000 ft MSL

### Where Transponder/ADS-B Required
- ✅ Class A, B, C airspace
- ✅ Within 30-NM **Mode C veil** of primary Class B airports
- ✅ Class E at and above **10,000 ft MSL**
- ❌ **Exclusion:** airspace at/below **2,500 ft AGL** (even if above 10,000 MSL)

### The 2,500 ft AGL Exclusion
- Example: terrain = 9,000 MSL, aircraft = 11,000 MSL (2,000 AGL)
- Above 10,000 MSL? **Yes** → BUT below 2,500 AGL → **EXEMPT**
- Purpose: accommodates mountain operations

> ⚠️ **Checkride Trap:** The 10,000 ft MSL rule has a hidden exclusion for aircraft at or below 2,500 ft AGL. This is a common DPE gotcha question.

required_knowledge_points.title: Using Electronic Navigation Systems — Tune-Identify-Twist, CDI Source, and GPS Programming
required_knowledge_points.why: The DPE tests your ability to physically operate the navigation equipment during the flight. The most common checkride failure here is using the wrong CDI source — programming a GPS waypoint but leaving the CDI slaved to VLOC, so you chase a dead VOR needle while the GPS course goes unfollowed.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: VOR OPERATION ('TUNE, IDENTIFY, TWIST'): (1) TUNE — dial the correct VHF frequency into the NAV standby window, then swap to active. (2) IDENTIFY — CRITICAL step. Pull the NAV volume knob and listen for the Morse code identifier. If absent or wrong, the signal is illegal to use. (3) TWIST — rotate the OBS to align the desired course with the top index. GPS OPERATION: (1) Power up and acknowledge database currency/RAIM status. (2) Use 'Direct-To' or 'Flight Plan' function to program destination. (3) VERIFY — when typing 'KORD', confirm the spelled-out name ('CHICAGO OHARE INTL') before executing. Failure = 'Garbage In, Garbage Out.' CDI SOURCE BUTTON: on Garmin 430/530/G1000, the CDI source button toggles between VLOC (VOR/Localizer) and GPS. If the pilot programs a GPS waypoint but leaves the CDI on VLOC, the CDI needle responds to the VOR — NOT the GPS. The pilot chases an irrelevant VOR needle while the GPS track goes unmonitored. This is a COMMON checkride failure. COURSE INTERCEPTION: set the desired course on the OBS. If CDI deflects left = course is to the left. Turn to a 30-45° intercept heading into the deflection. Hold heading until the needle begins centering. Lead the turn to roll out on course as the needle centers. TRACKING (BRACKETING): once on course, if the needle drifts, apply a 10° correction into the drift. When the needle re-centers, take out half the correction. If the needle stays centered, you've found the wind correction angle.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### VOR: Tune, Identify, Twist
| Step | Action | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **TUNE** | Dial frequency into NAV radio | Get on the right station |
| **IDENTIFY** | Listen for **Morse code** | Confirm station is valid — maintenance mode = NO ident |
| **TWIST** | Rotate OBS to desired course | Set up the CDI for tracking |

### GPS Programming Flow
```
1. Power up → acknowledge database/RAIM
2. Select Direct-To or Flight Plan
3. Type waypoint identifier (e.g., KORD)
4. VERIFY spelled-out name (CHICAGO OHARE INTL) ← CRITICAL
5. Execute → CDI slews to course
```

### CDI Source — The #1 Checkride Trap
| CDI Source | CDI Responds To |
|---|---|
| **VLOC** | VOR/Localizer (ground-based) |
| **GPS** | Satellite navigation |

⚠️ If you program a GPS waypoint but CDI is on **VLOC** → you're chasing a VOR needle, NOT your GPS course

### Course Interception & Bracketing
```
INTERCEPT: CDI deflects left → course is LEFT → turn 30-45° left
           Hold heading → watch needle move toward center
           Lead the turn → roll out on course as needle centers

BRACKET:   Needle drifts left → wind pushes right → correct 10° left
           Needle re-centers → remove half correction (5° right)
           Needle stays centered → WCA found ✓
```

> ⚠️ **Checkride Trap:** ALWAYS check the CDI source button (VLOC vs GPS) BEFORE tracking any course. Wrong source = wrong needle = wrong direction.

lesson_overview:
## Transponders, ADS-B, Radar Services, and Electronic Navigation Skills

This lesson covers the surveillance technology that makes aircraft visible to ATC, the radar services available to VFR pilots, and the physical skills required to operate electronic navigation systems during flight.

**The ATC surveillance system fuses two distinct radar technologies.** Primary radar bounces radio energy off the aircraft's metallic skin — a passive technique requiring no aircraft equipment. Secondary radar (ATCRBS) sends an interrogation pulse that triggers an active reply from the aircraft's transponder, providing a discrete identification code and pressure altitude. The secondary system is vastly more reliable, offers greater range, and eliminates weather and ground clutter from the controller's scope. Mode A provides identification, Mode C adds altitude, and Mode S enables selective interrogation and forms the backbone of TCAS collision avoidance. ADS-B Out represents the next generation: the aircraft continuously broadcasts its GPS-derived position, altitude, velocity, and Flight ID to ground stations and other equipped aircraft, eliminating the geometry limitations of ground-based radar entirely.

**VFR Flight Following is the most commonly misunderstood ATC service.** It provides traffic advisories, safety alerts, and a discrete squawk code — all on a workload-permitting basis. Controllers can terminate the service at any time, and the pilot retains full responsibility for see-and-avoid, terrain clearance, and weather avoidance. The most dangerous misunderstanding: Flight Following does NOT constitute a clearance into Class B airspace. The pilot must hear the explicit words 'Cleared into the Class Bravo airspace' before penetrating the boundary. Another trap: ATC traffic calls reference the aircraft's radar ground track, not its magnetic heading. In a crosswind with a significant crab angle, traffic called at '12 o'clock' by the controller may appear well off to the side of the aircraft.

**Operating electronic navigation equipment requires both procedural knowledge and physical skill.** VOR operation follows the Tune-Identify-Twist sequence. The Identify step — listening for the Morse code identifier — is the most critical and most commonly skipped. A VOR in maintenance mode transmits a signal that centers the CDI without transmitting an identifier, creating a trap that sends trusting pilots off course. GPS operation demands waypoint verification before execution — typing an identifier and pressing Enter without confirming the spelled-out name is the definition of 'Garbage In, Garbage Out.' The single most common checkride failure in this task area is the CDI source mismatch: programming a GPS waypoint but leaving the CDI slaved to VLOC, causing the pilot to track a VOR needle while the GPS course goes unmonitored. Course interception requires geometric understanding (the CDI deflection direction tells you where the course is), and course tracking requires the bracketing technique to find the wind correction angle.
